headings.title: Introduction and Definition of the Intravenous Route
headings.content: The intravenous (IV) route involves delivering medications, fluids, and blood products directly into a patient's venous circulation. Bypassing the digestive tract and tissue absorption barriers, this method places active substances immediately into the bloodstream. Peak plasma concentrations occur almost instantly, making the route indispensable in critical care, emergency resuscitation, and severe dehydration management. Nurses rely on IV access when oral administration is impossible, gastrointestinal absorption is unreliable, or an immediate systemic response is required.

headings.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Intravenous Therapy
headings.content:
Intravenous therapy offers distinct clinical benefits alongside notable hazards that demand vigilant nursing oversight.

- **Rapid onset**: Immediate therapeutic availability makes it ideal for emergencies.
- **Precise dosing**: Titration allows exact control over blood levels.
- **Gastrointestinal bypass**: Useful for patients with severe vomiting or malabsorption.
- **Systemic toxicity risk**: Mistakes in administration speed or dose cannot be retrieved once injected.
- **Infection potential**: Breaks in skin integrity invite local and systemic pathogens.
- **Fluid overload**: Rapid or excessive infusion strains the cardiovascular system.

headings.title: Anatomical Sites and Vein Selection for Venipuncture
headings.content: Selecting an appropriate venipuncture site minimizes complications and ensures successful cannulation. Nurses typically begin with the distal veins of the upper extremities, progressing proximally if new sites are needed. Common choices include the metacrapal, cephalic, and basilic veins of the hand and forearm. Lower extremity veins are generally avoided in adults due to the high risk of thrombophlebitis and sluggish circulation. Veins that feel firm, tortuous, or lie near known arteries and nerve pathways must be bypassed.

headings.title: Equipment and Materials Needed for IV Cannulation
headings.content:
Gathering supplies before entering the patient's room ensures a smooth and sterile procedure. Essential items include:

- **IV cannula (Catheter over needle)**: Sized appropriately for the patient and vein.
- **Tourniquet**: Used to distend veins by impeding venous return.
- **Antiseptic swab**: Chlorhexidine or alcohol for skin disinfection.
- **Transparent dressing**: Secures the catheter and allows site inspection.
- **Extension set and flush**: Maintains line patency and connection safety.
- **Personal protective equipment**: Clean gloves protect both patient and nurse.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Initiating IV Access
headings.content: Initiating intravenous access requires precision, aseptic technique, and clear communication with the patient. Explain the procedure, verify identity, and position the patient comfortably. Apply the tourniquet and select a straight, bouncy vein. Cleanse the skin using a friction scrub and allow it to air dry completely. Anchor the vein with your non-dominant hand, insert the needle at a 15 to 30-degree angle, and watch for flashback. Once blood appears, lower the cannula parallel to the skin, advance it slightly, retract the needle while advancing the plastic catheter, release the tourniquet, attach the extension tubing, and secure the site.

headings.title: Methods of IV Administration: Bolus, Infusion, and Piggyback
headings.content: Medications enter the bloodstream through various techniques depending on dosage requirements and drug characteristics. An IV push or bolus delivers a concentrated dose directly into the vein or injection port over a short duration, requiring careful monitoring for adverse reactions. Continuous infusions administer large volumes of fluids or medications at a steady, controlled rate over hours or days. Intermittent infusions, commonly known as piggyback setups, deliver a secondary medication through an existing primary line at scheduled intervals.

headings.title: Calculation of IV Flow Rates and Infusion Doses
headings.content:
Calculating accurate infusion rates prevents both fluid overload and under-medication. Nurses must master the formula for gravity drips based on drop factor, as well as electronic pump programming in milliliters per hour. 

$$\text{Flow Rate (gtt/min)} = \frac{\text{Volume (mL)} \times \text{Drop Factor (gtt/mL)}}{\text{Time (minutes)}}$|

Always double-check calculations and verify drug concentrations with a colleague when managing high-alert medications.

headings.title: Monitoring, Maintenance, and Complications of IV Therapy
headings.content:
Constant vigilance preserves vascular access and protects patients from localized and systemic injury. Inspect insertion sites routinely for signs of infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, or local infection. Flush intermittent lines with saline to prevent clotting and maintain patency. 

| Complication | Key Characteristic |
| --- | --- |
| Infiltration | Swelling, coolness, and pallor around the site |
| Phlebitis | Erythema, warmth, and a palpable cord along the vein |
| Extravasation | Pain, burning, and tissue necrosis from vesicant drugs |
| Air Embolism | Sudden respiratory distress, hypotension, and cyanosis |

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities and Patient Safety Guidelines
headings.content: Safe intravenous therapy rests on adherence to professional standards and institutional safety protocols. Nurses must verify the five rights of medication administration before every infusion. Sterile technique must remain unbroken during tubing changes, dressing replacements, and site care. Educate patients to report pain, burning, or wetness at the site immediately. Document insertion details, site assessments, fluid totals, and discontinuation times accurately in the clinical record.
